summary:
Alabama is a state of the United States and stands under the national framework carried at the country level.

Facility access is the most immediate state-level exposure. The Movement Advancement Project's equality map records Alabama as enacting bans on transgender people using public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity in 2022 and 2024. House Bill 322, signed 8 April 2022 as Act No. 2022-290 and codified by the Alabama Board of Education in September 2022, requires public school students to use bathrooms consistent with the gender recorded on their birth certificate. A March 2024 bill would extend this to ban university bathroom use not aligned with sex assigned at birth, and the Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update records that Alabama's 'Don't Say Gay' bill carries a bathroom ban extending to college campuses, placing the state in the assessment's worst-law grouping of legislatively-erasing jurisdictions. Senate Bill 79, signed February 2025, declares gender an immutable male-female binary determined by biological sex assigned at birth and allows separate single-sex spaces where biology, privacy, safety or fairness are implicated.

Gender-affirming care for minors is criminalised. Since 8 May 2022 the Vulnerable Child Compassion and Protection Act (SB 184), signed 8 April 2022, makes it a Class C felony punishable by 10 years in prison for a medical provider to give puberty blockers, hormones, or surgeries to anyone under 19. The Eleventh Circuit allowed enforcement from 21 August 2023, and the ban remained in force after plaintiffs withdrew their challenge on 1 May 2025.

Identity documents carry a surgery requirement. Alabama permits amendment of birth certificates and driver's licences to current sex only with documentation of sex "changed by surgical procedure" and a name change. In Corbitt v. Taylor a January 2021 federal ruling invalidated the surgery requirement, but the Eleventh Circuit reversed this, leaving the requirement standing; on 20 September 2024 the Eleventh Circuit ruled that refusal to issue accurate licences did not violate the federal constitution, rehearing was denied 13 November 2024, and judgment was entered 10 December 2024. The ACLU states that most transgender people therefore cannot obtain an accurate licence and must carry daily ID showing the wrong gender, exposing them to harassment and violence in ID checks.

Sports participation is restricted by sex assigned at birth. Since 1 July 2021 public schools must assign single-sex sports teams by "biological sex," and House Bill 391, enacted April 2021 after passing the House 74-19 with two abstentions and signed by Governor Kay Ivey, requires all K-12 athletes to compete based on the gender listed on their birth certificate. House Bill 261, signed 30 May 2023, prohibits college and university competition on a team differing from sex assigned at birth even after gender-affirming hormone therapy, except in co-ed sports.

No statewide nondiscrimination protection exists. State law provides no prohibition on discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations, or student harassment and bullying; there is no ban on insurance exclusions for transgender healthcare and no transgender-inclusive health benefits for state employees. Only Birmingham (since September 2017) and Montevallo (since April 2018) prohibit all such discrimination, while Huntsville, Tuscaloosa and Montgomery provide public-employment protections. As of 2025, statewide polling places Alabama among the lowest-support states for transgender-inclusive nondiscrimination and access policies, leaving trans visitors without statewide public-accommodations recourse and exposed to denial of care for accompanying minors, exclusion from gendered facilities and sports, and ID incongruence in ID checks.

Hate-crime law does not cover gender identity. Alabama's hate-crime law since 1994 covers only race, color, religion, national origin, ethnicity, or physical or mental disability. Gender identity has been applied to sex under Title VII in Eleventh Circuit jurisdiction since 2011, and the federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, signed October 2009, bans gender-identity hate crimes federally.

Marriage recognition has improved on paper. Same-sex marriage became legal nationwide 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, but eight Alabama counties still refused all marriage licenses by 2017, until the Legislature in May 2019 required recording of marriage certificates and all counties began recording for all couples including same-sex couples on 29 August 2019, leaving the 1996 Executive Order Number 24, the 1998 statute Alabama Code § 30-1-19, and the June 2006 constitutional Amendment 774 unenforceable.

Adoption is permitted for same-sex couples, though the Supreme Court of Alabama in 2002 held homosexual conduct created a strong presumption of parental unfitness as "abhorrent, immoral, detestable," and the May 2017 Child Placing Agency Inclusion Act signed by Governor Kay Ivey protects faith-based agencies refusing placements on religious beliefs.
tangentialFactors:
Alabama's regime sits within a national pattern of tightening state-level restrictions. The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 update places Alabama in its worst-law grouping of legislatively-erasing jurisdictions, alongside other states flagged for bathroom bans and document restrictions.

The Eleventh Circuit's rulings in Corbitt v. Taylor and its September 2024 decision upholding refusal of accurate licences reflect a broader appellate posture in this circuit that differs from other federal circuits on trans document rights.

Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in Alabama since the 2003 Lawrence v. Texas decision striking down sodomy laws, and Alabama Senate Bill 320, passed by the House 23 May 2019 by 101 yes with 3 absent and by the Senate 28 May 2019 by 32 yea with 3 absent, repealed the state's ban on "deviate sexual intercourse" effective 1 September 2019; the age of consent is 16 with a within-2-years exception extended to same-sex contact in 2019.

From 1992 to 2021 Alabama law required sexual education to emphasize "that homosexuality is not a lifestyle acceptable to the general public and that homosexual conduct is a criminal offense," repealed in April 2021 after Governor Kay Ivey signed repeal of archaic references to homosexuality and HIV/AIDS.

outOfScopeNotes:
The Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map's July 2026 grouping of Alabama as a legislatively-erasing jurisdiction is a third-party assessment; the underlying 'Don't Say Gay' bill text and its precise campus-bathroom provisions are not reproduced in this inventory and remain unverified here.

The March 2024 university bathroom bill's final legislative status is not stated in the inventory; whether it was enacted, amended, or failed is unresolved.

The inventory does not document any specific incident of violence against a trans person in Alabama, nor any trans-specific crime rate for the state, so no comparative violence risk can be stated.

Whether the May 2019 legislative requirement that all counties record marriage certificates has been fully complied with in every county since 29 August 2019 is not independently verified beyond the source's statement.
